messages.subject: a few questions around DRF
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

Thank you once again for the great feedback and support on the mirt package! I am working on analysing literacy achievement data using the DRF statistics and have a few questions I'd very much appreciate your help with. Apologies for any questions that are naive.

Here's a sample of the syntax or reference:

model_anchorpoetrysocialmediasongs<- multipleGroup(DIF1and6items, model = Q1, group = grouppoetrysocialmediasongs,
                                                   invariance = c(itemnames[c(6:11,41)],
                                                                  'free_means', 'free_var'), SE=T)

dialogDRF2poetrysocialmediasongs= DRF(model_anchorpoetrysocialmediasongs, focal_items = c(21:25,42,43), plot = F,draws=500)
dialogDRF2poetrysocialmediasongs

Output:
     n_focal_items        stat      CI_2.5     CI_97.5        X2 df           p
sDRF             7 -0.07664762 -0.15114407 0.004747429  3.900895  1 0.048260391
uDRF             7  0.13499792  0.06517565 0.213141560 12.366079  2 0.002064145

(Please also see attached plot of this output).

1. If I understand correctly, the 2018 Psychometrika article ("Model-based"...) suggests that non-studied items are included in the DRF analyses. Can you please explain a bit further how non-studied items are included? In the provided syntax I understand they are used for modeling the configural MG model as separate groups but I am not sure how they are included in the DRF analysis.

2. Can inferences about both difficulty and discrimination be generated based on these sDRF and uDRF statistics / attached plot? Or just difficulty?

3. Are sDRF and uDRF statistics calculated as the average across entire theta? (I read that a subset of theta can be calculated instead but I wanted to be sure.) And, are the uDRF and sDRF stats printed above effect sizes that can be interpreted similarly to Cohen's d?

4. If the focal group selection is arbitrary, do I assume a negatively signed value of sDRF as above refers to invariance in favor of group 1 (the reference group)?

5. In the attached plot, which is related to the above output, the values on higher levels of theta appear to be more reliable. These are biased in favor of group 1 (the reference group), correct? As the area under the curve is greater on the lower end of theta (in favor of focal group), is it the lack of accuracy in the lower region of theta that makes the overall sDRF in favor of the reference group? Is this what is meant by marginal density of the latent trait distribution (here, that there are few cases with very low theta values)?

6. Lastly, I have five groups, one of which is reference. I have run independent IRT models like the one above for each group and then subsequent DRF for each bundle for each 2-group IRT model. Is that the correct procedure for multiple groups?

Thank you!
Jeanne

> Hi Phil,
>
> Thank you once again for the great feedback and support on the mirt package! I am working on analysing literacy achievement data using the DRF statistics and have a few questions I'd very much appreciate your help with. Apologies for any questions that are naive.
>
> Here's a sample of the syntax or reference:
>
> model_anchorpoetrysocialmediasongs<- multipleGroup(DIF1and6items, model = Q1, group = grouppoetrysocialmediasongs,
>                                                    invariance = c(itemnames[c(6:11,41)],
>                                                                   'free_means', 'free_var'), SE=T)
>
> dialogDRF2poetrysocialmediasongs= DRF(model_anchorpoetrysocialmediasongs, focal_items = c(21:25,42,43), plot = F,draws=500)
> dialogDRF2poetrysocialmediasongs
>
> Output:
>      n_focal_items        stat      CI_2.5     CI_97.5        X2 df           p
> sDRF             7 -0.07664762 -0.15114407 0.004747429  3.900895  1 0.048260391
> uDRF             7  0.13499792  0.06517565 0.213141560 12.366079  2 0.002064145
>
> (Please also see attached plot of this output).
>
> 1. If I understand correctly, the 2018 Psychometrika article ("Model-based"...) suggests that non-studied items are included in the DRF analyses. Can you please explain a bit further how non-studied items are included? In the provided syntax I understand they are used for modeling the configural MG model as separate groups but I am not sure how they are included in the DRF analysis.

Non-studied items are really just auxiliary information and don't play a part in the model other than improving statistical power and introducing bias/less efficiency in the estimates. These have been present in many other analysis as well (like those in the DIF() function), in that they represent all the items in a fitted IRT model that were not in the focal set (the item to test for DIF) and anchor set (the items explicitly declared as anchors in the fitted model). I wouldn't worry much about this one, I just needed to give them a name to contrast these with the SIBTEST approach.

>
> 2. Can inferences about both difficulty and discrimination be generated based on these sDRF and uDRF statistics / attached plot? Or just difficulty?

Neither. These are about the *model-implied bias*, and are detached from any parameter interpretation. That's what makes them so nice for effect size interpretation, because sDRF always represents the average scoring between groups for a given (set) of items, while uDRF is the average deviation bias between the given (set) of items.

>
> 3. Are sDRF and uDRF statistics calculated as the average across entire theta? (I read that a subset of theta can be calculated instead but I wanted to be sure.) And, are the uDRF and sDRF stats printed above effect sizes that can be interpreted similarly to Cohen's d?

Effectively, you can interpreted them as such. For example, a uDRF = 0.1 with only one focal item (i.e., DIF) says that the item response functions will differ on average by about .1 points. So at any given location across the range of theta, we would expect the two groups to show a scoring different of 0.1. The same interpretation exists for sDRF, but with respect to the balance of scoring form.

>
> 4. If the focal group selection is arbitrary, do I assume a negatively signed value of sDRF as above refers to invariance in favor of group 1 (the reference group)?

Correct.

>
> 5. In the attached plot, which is related to the above output, the values on higher levels of theta appear to be more reliable. These are biased in favor of group 1 (the reference group), correct? As the area under the curve is greater on the lower end of theta (in favor of focal group), is it the lack of accuracy in the lower region of theta that makes the overall sDRF in favor of the reference group? Is this what is meant by marginal density of the latent trait distribution (here, that there are few cases with very low theta values)?

This plot is really the conditional bias effect of of bias across theta, whereas the DRF statistics try to marginalize this entire response function into single statistics (and may do so poorly). Hence, uDRF is telling you the average difference between these functions, while sDRF is telling you the average while allowing for cancellation effects (hence, the global scoring bias observed....which could potentially cancel out as nearly happens in this plot, and is why sDRF was so close to 0 in your output).

>
> 6. Lastly, I have five groups, one of which is reference. I have run independent IRT models like the one above for each group and then subsequent DRF for each bundle for each 2-group IRT model. Is that the correct procedure for multiple groups?

For now, yes. I'm working on many extensions to this work, one of which is incorporating more than two groups at once. But for now, there's nothing really wrong with your approach, and in many ways is quite favorable. HTH.

Phil

> Thank you!
> Jeanne

On Mon, Jul 2, 2018 at 11:04 AM Jeanne Sinclair <jeanneh...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> Is this scoring difference on just the focal items, e.g., 0.1 point higher/lower with regard to the 7 focal items (not all items modeled in the original MG IRT model)?

Correct, only in the focal item set. So you need to keep in mind the size of this bundle to determine what the magitude actually represents. E.g. a value of .1 for a focal item set with 10 dichotomous items appears rather small, but for a focal item set with 1 item would probably be considered quite large.

>
> Does this interpretation hold for polytomous items? I noticed the MG output indicates that "Item re-scored so that all values are within a distance of 1” — does this take care of the interpretation of the effect size for polytomous items?

Sure does. For polytomous items these are with respect to the item scoring function, which is the generalisation of the probability interpretation for dichotomous items (the scoring and probability functions for dichotomous items are identical).

messages.subject: Re: a few questions around DRF
messages.body_plain:
Hello again, me with more questions... sorry for the trouble. Kind of more on a theoretical level, I ran a unidimensional multiple group model with reference means and variances constrained, with anchors, and had good model fit in terms of TLI, CLI, RMSEA, and SRMSR. The DRF analyses have been based on that model. Things have been going pretty well.

But, I've been reading up on the work of Roussos and Stout, and it seems a major advantage DRF has is that it can base the bias analysis on a true multidimensional model, whereas SIBTEST (if I understand correctly) could identify dimensions through other means (prior to DBF analysis), but, ultimately, statistically, the analysis for SIBTEST did not take multidimensionality into consideration for actual DBF analysis -- as it wasn't model-based, I guess it wasn't a possibility (is that correct?). I was looking at Roussos and Stout (1996) and they talk about the marginalized item response functions for the two dimensions, but I am not sure SIBTEST actually models that?  Anyway, I was wondering if you think running a unidimensional model is appropriate for DRF, given that the nuisance dimensions are, well, dimensions that might need to be modeled at the MG level. Would it be appropriate to more iteratively see where DRF occurs in unidimensional model and then go back and try to refine the multiple group model with those multiple dimensions, and rerun the DRF? Sort of thinking in circles here but would like to hear your thoughts on this. Thanks!

> > >

> > Correct, only in the focal item set. So you need to keep in mind the size of this bundle to determine what the magitude actually represents. E.g. a value of .1 for a focal item set with 10 dichotomous items appears rather small, but for a focal item set with 1 item would probably be considered quite large.

> > > > >
> > > > > Here's a sample of the syntax or reference:
> > > > >
> > > > > model_anchorpoetrysocialmediasongs<- multipleGroup(DIF1and6items, model = Q1, group = grouppoetrysocialmediasongs,

> > > > >                                                                   'free_means', 'free_var'), SE=T)
> > > > >
> > > > > dialogDRF2poetrysocialmediasongs= DRF(model_anchorpoetrysocialmediasongs, focal_items = c(21:25,42,43), plot = F,draws=500)
> > > > > dialogDRF2poetrysocialmediasongs
> > > > >
> > > > > Output:
> > > > >      n_focal_items        stat      CI_2.5     CI_97.5        X2 df           p
> > > > > sDRF             7 -0.07664762 -0.15114407 0.004747429  3.900895  1 0.048260391
> > > > > uDRF             7  0.13499792  0.06517565 0.213141560 12.366079  2 0.002064145
> > > > >
> > > > > (Please also see attached plot of this output).
> > > > >
> > > > > 1. If I understand correctly, the 2018 Psychometrika article ("Model-based"...) suggests that non-studied items are included in the DRF analyses. Can you please explain a bit further how non-studied items are included? In the provided syntax I understand they are used for modeling the configural MG model as separate groups but I am not sure how they are included in the DRF analysis.
> > > >
> > > > Non-studied items are really just auxiliary information and don't play a part in the model other than improving statistical power and introducing bias/less efficiency in the estimates. These have been present in many other analysis as well (like those in the DIF() function), in that they represent all the items in a fitted IRT model that were not in the focal set (the item to test for DIF) and anchor set (the items explicitly declared as anchors in the fitted model). I wouldn't worry much about this one, I just needed to give them a name to contrast these with the SIBTEST approach.
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > 2. Can inferences about both difficulty and discrimination be generated based on these sDRF and uDRF statistics / attached plot? Or just difficulty?
> > > >
> > > > Neither. These are about the *model-implied bias*, and are detached from any parameter interpretation. That's what makes them so nice for effect size interpretation, because sDRF always represents the average scoring between groups for a given (set) of items, while uDRF is the average deviation bias between the given (set) of items.
> > > >
> > > >

> > > > >
> > > > > 3. Are sDRF and uDRF statistics calculated as the average across entire theta? (I read that a subset of theta can be calculated instead but I wanted to be sure.) And, are the uDRF and sDRF stats printed above effect sizes that can be interpreted similarly to Cohen's d?
> > > >
> > > > Effectively, you can interpreted them as such. For example, a uDRF = 0.1 with only one focal item (i.e., DIF) says that the item response functions will differ on average by about .1 points. So at any given location across the range of theta, we would expect the two groups to show a scoring different of 0.1. The same interpretation exists for sDRF, but with respect to the balance of scoring form.
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > 4. If the focal group selection is arbitrary, do I assume a negatively signed value of sDRF as above refers to invariance in favor of group 1 (the reference group)?
> > > >
> > > > Correct.
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > 5. In the attached plot, which is related to the above output, the values on higher levels of theta appear to be more reliable. These are biased in favor of group 1 (the reference group), correct? As the area under the curve is greater on the lower end of theta (in favor of focal group), is it the lack of accuracy in the lower region of theta that makes the overall sDRF in favor of the reference group? Is this what is meant by marginal density of the latent trait distribution (here, that there are few cases with very low theta values)?
> > > >
> > > > This plot is really the conditional bias effect of of bias across theta, whereas the DRF statistics try to marginalize this entire response function into single statistics (and may do so poorly). Hence, uDRF is telling you the average difference between these functions, while sDRF is telling you the average while allowing for cancellation effects (hence, the global scoring bias observed....which could potentially cancel out as nearly happens in this plot, and is why sDRF was so close to 0 in your output).
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > 6. Lastly, I have five groups, one of which is reference. I have run independent IRT models like the one above for each group and then subsequent DRF for each bundle for each 2-group IRT model. Is that the correct procedure for multiple groups?
> > > >
> > > > For now, yes. I'm working on many extensions to this work, one of which is incorporating more than two groups at once. But for now, there's nothing really wrong with your approach, and in many ways is quite favorable. HTH.
> > > >
> > > > Phil
> > > >

> > > > > Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
In the multipleGroup() approach all groups need to have qualitative separation, so you'd have to create a new single grouping variable that represents the combination of these four levels. E.g.,

gender <- factor(rep(c('Male', 'Female'), each=5))
age <- factor(rep(c('Young', 'Old'), times=5))

newgroup <- gender:age
newgroup
table(newgroup)

Phil

I was looking at Roussos and Stout (1996) and they talk about the marginalized item response functions for the two dimensions, but I am not sure SIBTEST actually models that?

They don't, and it's a rather confusing part of that liturature. Basically, if DIF is detected then there must be some version of multidimensional present (whether that be from extraneous causal factors, other abilities, ect). Hence, the DRF statistics have the same type of interpretation, which shouldn't be surprising since the SIBTEST measures are really classical test theory approaches to what the DRF measure obtain through model fitting.

> Anyway, I was wondering if you think running a unidimensional model is appropriate for DRF, given that the nuisance dimensions are, well, dimensions that might need to be modeled at the MG level. Would it be appropriate to more iteratively see where DRF occurs in unidimensional model and then go back and try to refine the multiple group model with those multiple dimensions, and rerun the DRF? Sort of thinking in circles here but would like to hear your thoughts on this. Thanks!

Different questions really. Modeling multidimensionality is a very different task than bias testing....and with it's own set of problems. The DRF stats could work for multidimensional IRT models, but not without some headaches related to numerical integration as well. HTH.

Phil

I wouldn't worry much about this one, I just needed to give them a name to contrast these with the SIBTEST approach.
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 2. Can inferences about both difficulty and discrimination be generated based on these sDRF and uDRF statistics / attached plot? Or just difficulty?
> > > > >
> > > > > Neither. These are about the *model-implied bias*, and are detached from any parameter interpretation. That's what makes them so nice for effect size interpretation, because sDRF always represents the average scoring between groups for a given (set) of items, while uDRF is the average deviation bias between the given (set) of items.
> > > > >
> > > > >

> > > > > >
> > > > > > 3. Are sDRF and uDRF statistics calculated as the average across entire theta? (I read that a subset of theta can be calculated instead but I wanted to be sure.) And, are the uDRF and sDRF stats printed above effect sizes that can be interpreted similarly to Cohen's d?
> > > > >
> > > > > Effectively, you can interpreted them as such. For example, a uDRF = 0.1 with only one focal item (i.e., DIF) says that the item response functions will differ on average by about .1 points. So at any given location across the range of theta, we would expect the two groups to show a scoring different of 0.1. The same interpretation exists for sDRF, but with respect to the balance of scoring form.
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 4. If the focal group selection is arbitrary, do I assume a negatively signed value of sDRF as above refers to invariance in favor of group 1 (the reference group)?
> > > > >
> > > > > Correct.
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 5. In the attached plot, which is related to the above output, the values on higher levels of theta appear to be more reliable. These are biased in favor of group 1 (the reference group), correct? As the area under the curve is greater on the lower end of theta (in favor of focal group), is it the lack of accuracy in the lower region of theta that makes the overall sDRF in favor of the reference group? Is this what is meant by marginal density of the latent trait distribution (here, that there are few cases with very low theta values)?
> > > > >
> > > > > This plot is really the conditional bias effect of of bias across theta, whereas the DRF statistics try to marginalize this entire response function into single statistics (and may do so poorly). Hence, uDRF is telling you the average difference between these functions, while sDRF is telling you the average while allowing for cancellation effects (hence, the global scoring bias observed....which could potentially cancel out as nearly happens in this plot, and is why sDRF was so close to 0 in your output).
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 6. Lastly, I have five groups, one of which is reference. I have run independent IRT models like the one above for each group and then subsequent DRF for each bundle for each 2-group IRT model. Is that the correct procedure for multiple groups?
> > > > >
> > > > > For now, yes. I'm working on many extensions to this work, one of which is incorporating more than two groups at once. But for now, there's nothing really wrong with your approach, and in many ways is quite favorable. HTH.
> > > > >
> > > > > Phil
> > > > >

> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thank you!
> > > > > > Jeanne

Great, thanks Phil, that does make sense. To me it seems a fuzzy area, the question of intentional versus unintentional multidimensionality (Oshima et al), or auxiliary vs. nuisiance/ benign vs. adverse (Roussos & Stout).... e.g., what should be modeled. I guess I need to do some more thinking. Thanks as always for the great feedback!

Kind of more on a theoretical level, I ran a unidimensional multiple group model with reference means and variances constrained, with anchors, and had good model fit in terms of TLI, CLI, RMSEA, and SRMSR. The DRF analyses have been based on that model. Things have been going pretty well.
> >
> > But, I've been reading up on the work of Roussos and Stout, and it seems a major advantage DRF has is that it can base the bias analysis on a true multidimensional model, whereas SIBTEST (if I understand correctly) could identify dimensions through other means (prior to DBF analysis), but, ultimately, statistically, the analysis for SIBTEST did not take multidimensionality into consideration for actual DBF analysis -- as it wasn't model-based, I guess it wasn't a possibility (is that correct?). I was looking at Roussos and Stout (1996) and they talk about the marginalized item response functions for the two dimensions, but I am not sure SIBTEST actually models that?
>
> They don't, and it's a rather confusing part of that liturature. Basically, if DIF is detected then there must be some version of multidimensional present (whether that be from extraneous causal factors, other abilities, ect). Hence, the DRF statistics have the same type of interpretation, which shouldn't be surprising since the SIBTEST measures are really classical test theory approaches to what the DRF measure obtain through model fitting.
>
> > Anyway, I was wondering if you think running a unidimensional model is appropriate for DRF, given that the nuisance dimensions are, well, dimensions that might need to be modeled at the MG level. Would it be appropriate to more iteratively see where DRF occurs in unidimensional model and then go back and try to refine the multiple group model with those multiple dimensions, and rerun the DRF? Sort of thinking in circles here but would like to hear your thoughts on this. Thanks!
>
> Different questions really. Modeling multidimensionality is a very different task than bias testing....and with it's own set of problems. The DRF stats could work for multidimensional IRT models, but not without some headaches related to numerical integration as well. HTH.
>
> Phil

messages.subject: Fscores from different objects
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

Thanks for your quick and previous answer.

I have a new question. Is it possible to  estimate factor scores from different models.

Let me explain and contextualize. OECD Pisa 2012 estimates Rasch/partial credit unidimensional model using 480000 observations based on 13 variables to create a home possession index. Additionally, estimates for each country a similar model with 3 variables, which are different for each country ( actually, in the technical report is not clear if they use those variables together or not).

After that, they estimate through WLE factor scores.

I've been trying to come with an idea to replicate the last step but don't know how to merge singleclass objects or extract information from them which could be used for the scores.

Any thoughts?

Thanks a lot,

Lucas

messages.subject: Re: bifactor EFA
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Jul 21, 2018 at 3:05 PM Elia Emmers <eliae...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Just a side not (to clarify my understanding a little bit) isn't this "ESEM" method just a very fancy name to say "rotated-loadings-now-with-standard-errors"?
>
> I've been reading the papers on Jennrich's rotation algorithms and I can't, for the life of me, figure out what the difference is from this new "modelling" technique of ESEM and a fancier rotation.

EFA usually goes 1) fit some arbitrary orthogonal solution with some identified pattern of loadings, and 2) rotate these loadings to something more meaningful based on some ad-hoc criteria (oblimin, promax, varimax, etc, including the rotations described by Jennrich). And because this is two step, you usually don't get things like SEs and other information, and it's harder to include auxiliary information in the form of covariates into the model. The ESEM approach tries to combine 1) and 2) at the same time, and tries to (cleverly) incorporate the rotation directly at the time of estimation. So, it's easier to nest the model in a SEM framework to do other things, like have other structural components.

I'm not really sure how much better it is from any practical sense, but it's a nice feature of ESEM that EFA can be somewhat nested into typical SEM software, and therefore it's easier to get things like goodness of fit tests and other prediction properties. HTH.

>
>
>
>

> > Yes, this is just a rotation that can be passed to the summary() function via the rotate argument after fitting an EFA. See the documentation for the supported rotations (all from the GPArotation package).
> >
> > Phil

messages.subject: Re: Bidimensional data simulation and recovery
messages.body_plain:
Your model is not identified (try passing SE=TRUE to mirt() to obtain the observed information matrix estimate). This part

model.2d <- mirt.model('
              F1 = 1-7
              F2 = 1-7
                     ')

should be changed to

model.2d <- mirt.model('
              F1 = 1-7

              F2 = 1-6
                     ')

So the last slope in the second dimension is constrained to 0 to fix the orientation. This is the default approach when using the numeric model input such as

mirt(data, model = 2)

which would be equivalent. This model is unique only up to a linear transformation, so you'd need to do a rotation after the model has converged in order to recover the original parameter structure.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Bidimensional data simulation and recovery
messages.body_plain:
Likely too little information to empirically identify a two-dimensional structure. Consider adding more items, or possibly increasing the sample size. Both should help with stability as they will increase the amount of statistical information available.

Note that rather than using your for() loops you could use the simdata() function from mirt, which will generate data much faster. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Bidimensional data simulation and recovery
messages.body_plain:
Ah, I see your problem here. For models where a mirt.model() interface has been supplied the rotate= argument is ignored in coef(), because it is assumed you fit a confirmatory model instead. To fix this, don't use your mirt.model() definition and instead just specify the number of factors to extract (in your case, 2). Then the rotate argument will be used since the mirt object is flagged as an exploratory IRT model. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Bidimensional data simulation and recovery
messages.body_plain:
coef(..., rotation = 'oblimin')

is quite different from

coef(..., rotate = 'oblimin')

The latter is the correct definition. See the documentation.

Phil

On Sun, Jul 22, 2018 at 5:36 PM Hugo Harada <hugo....@adaptativa.com.br> wrote:

> Hi, Phil!
>
> Ah, I see your problem here. For models where a mirt.model() interface has been supplied the rotate= argument is ignored in coef(), because it is assumed you fit a confirmatory model instead. To fix this, don't use your mirt.model() definition and instead just specify the number of factors to extract (in your case, 2). Then the rotate argument will be used since the mirt object is flagged as an exploratory IRT model. HTH.

messages.body_snippet:
coef(..., rotation = 'oblimin')

is quite different from

coef(..., rotate = 'oblimin')

The latter is the correct definition. See the documentation.

Phil

On Sun, Jul 22, 2018 at 5:36 PM Hugo Harada

messages.subject: Re: Bidimensional data simulation and recovery
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

Sorry for the mistake. Since the software did not complain that was a hard catch.

I re-ran the experiments and the recovery values tell the same story, d values are fine while a values are far from expected...I was expecting the oblimin rotation to give better results than varimax for correlated thetas but that does not seem to be the case...

Regards,

HUgo

messages.subject: Re: Bidimensional data simulation and recovery
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hugo,

Didn't you generate data with correlated theta values? The varimax rotation is orthogonal, so any ability differences would get absorbed into the a' coefficients. So something like oblimin would be a better choice (almost always....orthogonal rotations are needless strict for EFA purposes).

Phil

On Sun, Jul 22, 2018 at 8:55 PM Hugo Harada <hugo....@adaptativa.com.br> wrote:

> Dear Phil,
>
> Sorry for the mistake. Since the software did not complain that was a hard catch.
>
> I re-ran the experiments and the recovery values tell the same story, d values are fine while a values are far from expected...I was expecting the oblimin rotation to give better results than varimax for correlated thetas but that does not seem to be the case...
>
>
>
>
>
> Regards,
>
> HUgo
>
>
>
>

> 2018-07-22 18:47 GMT-03:00 Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com>:

> > coef(..., rotation = 'oblimin')
> >
> > is quite different from
> >
> > coef(..., rotate = 'oblimin')
> >
> > The latter is the correct definition. See the documentation.
> >
> > Phil
> >

> > On Sun, Jul 22, 2018 at 5:36 PM Hugo Harada <hugo....@adaptativa.com.br> wrote:

> > > Hi, Phil!
> > >
> > > Ah, I see your problem here. For models where a mirt.model() interface has been supplied the rotate= argument is ignored in coef(), because it is assumed you fit a confirmatory model instead. To fix this, don't use your mirt.model() definition and instead just specify the number of factors to extract (in your case, 2). Then the rotate argument will be used since the mirt object is flagged as an exploratory IRT model. HTH.
> > >
> > > I have rerun the experiments with model=2. This is what I've got.
> > >
> > > With covariânces set to 0, it seems that only d is recovered well.
> > > > mirt.fit = mirt(x, model=2, itemtype = '2PL', method = 'EM', SE=TRUE)
> > > > #getting coefficients
> > > > item.par.est=coef(mirt.fit,
> > > >                   rotation="varimax",
> > > >                   simplify=TRUE)
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > With covariances set to 0.4, I am having convergence issues, but the results are similar. Only d is recovered.
> > >
> > > > mirt.fit = mirt(x, model=2, itemtype = '2PL', method = 'EM', SE=TRUE)
> > > > #getting coefficients
> > > > item.par.est=coef(mirt.fit,
> > > >                   rotation="oblimin",
> > > >                   simplify=TRUE)
> > > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Regards,
> > >
> > > Hugo
> > >
> > > Code used is as below.
> > > --------------
> > >
> > >
> > > > rm(list=ls())
> > > >
> > > > library(MASS)
> > > > library(mirt)
> > > > library(rockchalk)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > ###Generate person parameters
> > > > N <- 10000
> > > > theta <- mvrnorm(n=N, mu=c(0,0), Sigma = lazyCor(0.4, 2) )
> > > > head(theta)
> > > > cor(theta)
> > > > summary(theta)
> > > > var(theta)
> > > >
> > > > ###Generate item parameters
> > > > n <- 7 #number of itens
> > > >
> > > > a1 <- runif(n,-0.5,1)
> > > > a2 <- runif(n,-0.5,1)
> > > > d <- rnorm(n,0,1)
> > > > item.par.sim <- cbind(a1,a2,d)
> > > >
> > > > ###Create arrays for prob (p) and simulated data (x)
> > > > p<-matrix(0,N,n)
> > > > x<-matrix(0,N,n)
> > > > colnames(x)<-c("i1","i2","i3","i4","i5","i6","i7")
> > > > ###Use a stochastic process to generate model-fitting data
> > > > for (i in 1:N) {
> > > >   for (j in 1:n){
> > > >     p[i,j] <- 1/(1+exp(-1*(a1[j]*theta[i,1]+a2[j]*theta[i,2]+d[j])))
> > > >     r <- runif(1,0,1)
> > > >     if (p[i,j]>=r) {
> > > >       x[i,j] <- 1 #individual answers correctly if p> 0.5
> > > >     }
> > > >   }
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > mirt.fit = mirt(x, model=2, itemtype = '2PL', method = 'EM', SE=TRUE)
> > > > #getting coefficients
> > > > item.par.est=coef(mirt.fit,
> > > >                   rotation="oblimin",
> > > >                   simplify=TRUE)
> > > > #checking parameter recovery
> > > > var(theta)
> > > > item.par.est$items
> > > > item.par.sim
> > > >
> > > > summary(mirt.fit)
> > >

messages.subject: Re: Bidimensional data simulation and recovery
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Phil.

Didn't you generate data with correlated theta values? The varimax rotation is orthogonal, so any ability differences would get absorbed into the a' coefficients. So something like oblimin would be a better choice (almost always....orthogonal rotations are needless strict for EFA purposes).

Yes, I did.

theta <- mvrnorm(n=N, mu=c(0,0), Sigma = lazyCor(0.4, 2) )

It baffles me how hard it is to get these a values recovered...Any other ideas?

Regards,

Hugo

messages.body_snippet:
Hi, Phil.

Didn't you generate data with correlated theta values? The varimax rotation is orthogonal, so any ability differences would get absorbed into the a' coefficients. So something like oblimin

messages.subject: Re: Bidimensional data simulation and recovery
messages.body_plain:
Use an oblique rotation. Or don't simulate with a correlation between the abilities.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Phil.

Use an oblique rotation. Or don't simulate with a correlation between the abilities.

That is the setup of one of the experiments of which I showed you the results. It is replicated below.  d values are fine while a values are far from expected. Not sure where the mistake can be now. Maybe I should built a version of the setup with your simdata() function...

Code is as below.

> rm(list=ls())
>
> library(MASS)
> library(mirt)
> library(rockchalk)
>
> ###Generate person parameters
> N <- 10000
>
> theta <- mvrnorm(n=N, mu=c(0,0), Sigma = lazyCor(0.4, 2) )
> head(theta)
> cor(theta)
> summary(theta)
> var(theta)
>
> ###Generate item parameters
> n <- 7 #number of itens
>
> a1 <- runif(n,-0.5,1)
> a2 <- runif(n,-0.5,1)
> d <- rnorm(n,0,1)
> item.par.sim <- cbind(a1,a2,d)
>
> ###Create arrays for prob (p) and simulated data (x)
> p<-matrix(0,N,n)
> x<-matrix(0,N,n)

> #colnames(x)<-c("i1","i2","i3","i4","i5","i6","i7","i8","i9","i10","i11","i12","i13","i14","i15","i16","i17","i18","i19","i20")

> colnames(x)<-c("i1","i2","i3","i4","i5","i6","i7")
> ###Use a stochastic process to generate model-fitting data
> for (i in 1:N) {
>   for (j in 1:n){
>     p[i,j] <- 1/(1+exp(-1*(a1[j]*theta[i,1]+a2[j]*theta[i,2]+d[j])))

>     if (p[i,j]>=r) {
>       x[i,j] <- 1 #individual answers correctly if p> 0.5
>     }
>   }
> }
>

> # model.2d <- mirt.model('
> #               F1 = 1-7

> #                      ')

> mirt.fit = mirt(x, model=2, itemtype = '2PL', method = 'EM', SE=TRUE)
> #getting coefficients

>                   rotate="oblimin",

>                   simplify=TRUE)
> #checking parameter recovery
> var(theta)
> item.par.est$items
> item.par.sim

Regards,

Hugo

messages.subject: Scoring of multiple answer items
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil, dear Community,

I'm currently trying to implement multiple choice items into mirtCat. In principle, everything works fine. I was able to load a csv-file with checkbox-questions and multiple options and multiple answers for each question. mirtCAT works just fine that far.
However, the scoring mirtCAT uses rewards every correct answer with one point, so that a question with three correct answers can give up to three point. At the same time checking wrong answers does not impact the score of the item.
What I would like to do is to: "Score an item with 1 point if and only if all correct answers are checked."

Example:
Which of the following are prime numbers:
Answer options: a)1 b)2 c)3 d)4 e)5
Correct answers: 2,3,5

Possible answer by a student #1: 1,2,3,5 -->results in 0 points
Possible answer by a student #2: 2,3,5 -->results in 1 points
Possible answer by a student #3: 2,3 -->results in 0 points

Is there any way to change the internal scoring of mirtCAT?

Thanks in advance for your help, it's really appreciated.

Best,

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: bifactor EFA
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Phil! I guess in most applied contexts I've only seen it as the measurement model part. So a simple CFA-type analysis with no other covariates. It was in that sense that I just started wondering "well, if you're neither adding any predictors like in MIMIC models nor any one-directional arrows... how is this different from an EFA with standard errors for the loadings?

On Saturday, July 21, 2018 at 12:38:30 PM UTC-7, Phil Chalmers wrote:

> EFA usually goes 1) fit some arbitrary orthogonal solution with some identified pattern of loadings, and 2) rotate these loadings to something more meaningful based on some ad-hoc criteria (oblimin, promax, varimax, etc, including the rotations described by Jennrich). And because this is two step, you usually don't get things like SEs and other information, and it's harder to include auxiliary information in the form of covariates into the model. The ESEM approach tries to combine 1) and 2) at the same time, and tries to (cleverly) incorporate the rotation directly at the time of estimation. So, it's easier to nest the model in a SEM framework to do other things, like have other structural components.
>
> I'm not really sure how much better it is from any practical sense, but it's a nice feature of ESEM that EFA can be somewhat nested into typical SEM software, and therefore it's easier to get things like goodness of fit tests and other prediction properties. HTH.
>

messages.subject: Re: Bidimensional data simulation and recovery
messages.body_plain:
I don't see any mistake here, this seems reasonable to me. You're trying to identify a set of loadings with very week effects (e.g., the slopes for item 7) and with very few items. Hence, there's going to be a lot of indeterminacy in locating the "true" generating model though exploratory means.

That said, these loading are fairly identifiable when the slopes are of a reasonable magnitude (closer to 1). If you multiply the first column of your item.par.est$items object by -1 then this looks fairly close to the population generating form (remember these are only unique up to linear transformations), while the second column seems reasonably close given the weak structural identification, The story here is that EFA is hard with only a few items, and even harder when the loading patterns are close to 0. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Scoring of multiple answer items
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

The argument AnswerFuns is exactly what you want here. The purpose of this list input is to specify how the observed responses are translated into suitable scoring forms for each respective item. Here's a trivial example reflecting how this works:

library(mirtCAT)
options <- matrix(c("Strongly Disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly Agree"),
                  nrow = 3, ncol = 5, byrow = TRUE)
questions <- c("Building CATs with mirtCAT is difficult.",
               "mirtCAT requires a substantial amount of coding.",
               "I would use mirtCAT in my research.")

df <- data.frame(Question = questions, Option=options, Type = 'checkbox')
AnswerFuns <- as.list(rep(NA, nrow(df)))
AnswerFuns[[1]] <- function(text) all(text %in% c("Strongly Disagree", "Disagree"))
AnswerFuns[[2]] <- function(text) all(text == "Neutral")
AnswerFuns[[3]] <- function(text) all(text == "Strongly Agree")

results <- mirtCAT(df = df, AnswerFuns=AnswerFuns)
summary(results)

The first question will only be given a 1 if the first two categories (and only the first two categories) are selected;  otherwise, it will give a 0 (note that TRUE and FALSE evaluate to 1 and 0 in R, respectively. Though you can use this idea to return other numbers as well). The next two functions really aren't needed since they are supported within the df object directly, but demonstrate how this same line of reasoning can be applied to other items in the pool. HTH, and let me know if you have any questions.

Phil

On Mon, Jul 23, 2018 at 9:39 AM Daniel Sommerhoff <daniel.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Phil, dear Community,
>
> I'm currently trying to implement multiple choice items into mirtCat. In principle, everything works fine. I was able to load a csv-file with checkbox-questions and multiple options and multiple answers for each question. mirtCAT works just fine that far.
> However, the scoring mirtCAT uses rewards every correct answer with one point, so that a question with three correct answers can give up to three point. At the same time checking wrong answers does not impact the score of the item.
> What I would like to do is to: "Score an item with 1 point if and only if all correct answers are checked."
>
> Example:
> Which of the following are prime numbers:
> Answer options: a)1 b)2 c)3 d)4 e)5
> Correct answers: 2,3,5

> Possible answer by a student #1: 1,2,3,5 -->results in 0 points
> Possible answer by a student #2: 2,3,5 -->results in 1 points
> Possible answer by a student #3: 2,3 -->results in 0 points
>
>
> Is there any way to change the internal scoring of mirtCAT?
>
> Thanks in advance for your help, it's really appreciated.

> Best,

2018-07-24 1:13 GMT-03:00 Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com>:

> I don't see any mistake here, this seems reasonable to me. You're trying to identify a set of loadings with very week effects (e.g., the slopes for item 7) and with very few items. Hence, there's going to be a lot of indeterminacy in locating the "true" generating model though exploratory means.
>
> That said, these loading are fairly identifiable when the slopes are of a reasonable magnitude (closer to 1). If you multiply the first column of your item.par.est$items object by -1 then this looks fairly close to the population generating form (remember these are only unique up to linear transformations), while the second column seems reasonably close given the weak structural identification, The story here is that EFA is hard with only a few items, and even harder when the loading patterns are close to 0. HTH.
>
> Phil
>

messages.subject: Re: Negative chi square values in DIF testing
messages.subject_clean: Negative chi square values in DIF testing
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

Sorry for the late response. I was in the middle of a move and only just now got back to this. I had the issue crop up again this time with some other comparison groups that previously had displayed full or partial metric invariance in SEM. One group appeared fine when testing DIF in all parameters but then had negative chi square values when testing individual parameters (White vs Asian DIF). The other had negative chi square values when testing all parameters and individual parameters (Het vs GB). I've attached data and syntax to help reproduce the issue.

Thanks,
Daniel

On Friday, June 22, 2018 at 8:32:58 PM UTC-4, Phil Chalmers wrote:
> My only guess here is as you imply; lack of convergence/termination issues (which can be more likely for graded response models) or a local minimum issue. For the clearly problematic items, you may have better luck explicitly fitting these nested models yourself to see if the problem can be isolated. That all said, if you can provide a simple reproducible example of this then I can try to see if the DIF() function can be made more robust to avoid issues like this in the future better.
>
> Phil
>
>
> On Fri, Jun 22, 2018 at 7:08 PM Daniel McKelvey <daniel.k...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Phil,
> >
> > I ran into some funky results in testing a measure for DIF where some of the DIF tests had negative chi-square values. My syntax is
> >
> > MvW_Wfreed = multipleGroup(MRNI_MvW_items, model, group = groups,
> >                                invariance = c('slopes', 'intercepts', 'free_means', 'free_var'),
> >                                technical = list(NCYCLES=5000))
> >
> > MvW_DIFtest = DIF(MvW_Wfreed, c('a1', 'd1', 'd2', 'd3', 'd4', 'd5', 'd6'), scheme = 'drop', technical = list(NCYCLES=5000))
> >
> > Most of the results look fine, but some came out like this:
> >
> > $M21
> >        AIC        AICc        SABIC       HQ           BIC       logLik         X2        df     p
> > 1 346235.6 346242.7 346769.5 346584.3 347243 -172968.8     NaN    NaN  NaN
> > 2 346272.3 346280.1 346831.3 346637.4 347327 -172980.1    -22.722   7     1
> >
> > Prior SEM tests of invariance indicated that metric invariance failed for all items in my comparison group, so I have a feeling that this could be the cause of the strange results. Still, I wanted to double check before I moved on.
> >
> > Thanks,
> > Daniel
> >

messages.subject: Some questions about the Generalized Graded Unfolding Model
messages.subject_clean: Some questions about the Generalized Graded Unfolding Model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

I am using the mirt package to analyze some questionnaire response data under the GGUM. I have several questions that I was hoping you could help me with:

1.) In the original paper where the model is described (http://www.ets.org/Media/Research/pdf/RR-98-32.pdf), in Figure 2 which shows the item tracelines, the x-axis is labelled as θ - δ. However, when using mirt to apply GGUM to scales from several questionnaires, the x-axis is labelled θ, although the curves generally follow the same shape as the curves in the original paper and it appears that they are using the same scale. I was wondering who is wrong here - for now I think that the original authors are wrong, since I think they incorrectly labelled the x-axis on the Figure 3. That figure shows the item characteristic curve and the x-axis is also labelled as θ - δ, although from what I understand the approximate quadratic shape of the item characteristic curve in GGUM should be a function of θ, not θ - δ. Can you clarify that it is the original authors who are wrong here (i.e., that they incorrectly labelled Figures 2 and 3, and not just the Figure 3)?

2.) I am dealing with the case where I'm unsure if the data conforms to the unidimensional unfolding model, or the two-dimensional linear (or at least, monotonic) model. In literature this is known as the "extra-factor phenomenon". I found a paper which explains that it is not possible to discern between the two models at the covariance-structure level (http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/01466216010251006). However, the paper goes on, if the data conforms to the unidimensional unfolding model, and not to the linear/monotonic model, and if it is analyzed through linear exploratory factor analysis with 2 factors, the scatterplot of the Bartlett factor scores of the two factors should be a (possibly rotated) parabola.

I simulated some data with mirt under the GGUM model using the simdata function and followed the procedure described above. However, the scatterplot of the Bartlett factor scores of the two factors doesn't quite resemble a parabola, although it does look like some sort of a concave curve. Do you have any thoughts on what could be going on here? Please see the image attached.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-iUEkUPWzGVI/W1nsw7Q4hTI/AAAAAAAACa4/E0BJFRVEmZ4UNi_WF_DrszUZcSMa0MM9ACLcBGAs/s1600/Image%2B26-07-2018%2Bat%2B16.42.jpg>

messages.subject_clean: Negative chi square values in DIF testing
messages.body_plain:
Patch for this issue has been added. This was mainly due to non-convergence of the submodels, which in hindsight could have been avoided by using a better optimizer by default (such as the nlminb optimizer, which is slower but more robust). This is now the default in DIF(), and the starting values are selected based on the initial nested model. Feel free to download for the fix.

Phil

On Thu, Jul 26, 2018 at 11:46 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dear Phil,
>
> I am using the mirt package to analyze some questionnaire response data under the GGUM. I have several questions that I was hoping you could help me with:
>
> 1.) In the original paper where the model is described (http://www.ets.org/Media/Research/pdf/RR-98-32.pdf), in Figure 2 which shows the item tracelines, the x-axis is labelled as θ - δ. However, when using mirt to apply GGUM to scales from several questionnaires, the x-axis is labelled θ, although the curves generally follow the same shape as the curves in the original paper and it appears that they are using the same scale. I was wondering who is wrong here - for now I think that the original authors are wrong, since I think they incorrectly labelled the x-axis on the Figure 3. That figure shows the item characteristic curve and the x-axis is also labelled as θ - δ, although from what I understand the approximate quadratic shape of the item characteristic curve in GGUM should be a function of θ, not θ - δ. Can you clarify that it is the original authors who are wrong here (i.e., that they incorrectly labelled Figures 2 and 3, and not just the Figure 3)?

I think they are both right. mirt's label indicates that the point of 0 probability occurs somewhere along theta, not necessarily where theta = 0, while Roberts just translates the x-axis to be centered right at the value of 0 by subtracting out the respective intercept terms. Hence, their graphic is just a shift in the x-axis.

>
> 2.) I am dealing with the case where I'm unsure if the data conforms to the unidimensional unfolding model, or the two-dimensional linear (or at least, monotonic) model. In literature this is known as the "extra-factor phenomenon". I found a paper which explains that it is not possible to discern between the two models at the covariance-structure level (http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/01466216010251006). However, the paper goes on, if the data conforms to the unidimensional unfolding model, and not to the linear/monotonic model, and if it is analyzed through linear exploratory factor analysis with 2 factors, the scatterplot of the Bartlett factor scores of the two factors should be a (possibly rotated) parabola.
>
> I simulated some data with mirt under the GGUM model using the simdata function and followed the procedure described above. However, the scatterplot of the Bartlett factor scores of the two factors doesn't quite resemble a parabola, although it does look like some sort of a concave curve. Do you have any thoughts on what could be going on here? Please see the image attached.

I don't think I'm familiar enough with the theory/reasoning of this method to offer anything meaningful. Perhaps others on this forum who are more familiar with the GGUM can offer some interpretation of this phenomenon?

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Some questions about the Generalized Graded Unfolding Model
messages.subject_clean: Some questions about the Generalized Graded Unfolding Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil!

Thank you for clarifying 1! That explanation actually makes perfect sense and I think it's exactly what's going on.

As for 2, I'm still hoping someone else will respond - if you know of anyone who has experience with GGUM, I would be very thankful if you would tell them about this problem.

Thanks!

On Saturday, July 28, 2018 at 7:43:48 PM UTC+1, Phil Chalmers wrote:
> On Thu, Jul 26, 2018 at 11:46 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Dear Phil,
> >
> > I am using the mirt package to analyze some questionnaire response data under the GGUM. I have several questions that I was hoping you could help me with:
> >
> > 1.) In the original paper where the model is described (http://www.ets.org/Media/Research/pdf/RR-98-32.pdf), in Figure 2 which shows the item tracelines, the x-axis is labelled as θ - δ. However, when using mirt to apply GGUM to scales from several questionnaires, the x-axis is labelled θ, although the curves generally follow the same shape as the curves in the original paper and it appears that they are using the same scale. I was wondering who is wrong here - for now I think that the original authors are wrong, since I think they incorrectly labelled the x-axis on the Figure 3. That figure shows the item characteristic curve and the x-axis is also labelled as θ - δ, although from what I understand the approximate quadratic shape of the item characteristic curve in GGUM should be a function of θ, not θ - δ. Can you clarify that it is the original authors who are wrong here (i.e., that they incorrectly labelled Figures 2 and 3, and not just the Figure 3)?
>
> I think they are both right. mirt's label indicates that the point of 0 probability occurs somewhere along theta, not necessarily where theta = 0, while Roberts just translates the x-axis to be centered right at the value of 0 by subtracting out the respective intercept terms. Hence, their graphic is just a shift in the x-axis.
>
> >
> > 2.) I am dealing with the case where I'm unsure if the data conforms to the unidimensional unfolding model, or the two-dimensional linear (or at least, monotonic) model. In literature this is known as the "extra-factor phenomenon". I found a paper which explains that it is not possible to discern between the two models at the covariance-structure level (http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/01466216010251006). However, the paper goes on, if the data conforms to the unidimensional unfolding model, and not to the linear/monotonic model, and if it is analyzed through linear exploratory factor analysis with 2 factors, the scatterplot of the Bartlett factor scores of the two factors should be a (possibly rotated) parabola.
> >
> > I simulated some data with mirt under the GGUM model using the simdata function and followed the procedure described above. However, the scatterplot of the Bartlett factor scores of the two factors doesn't quite resemble a parabola, although it does look like some sort of a concave curve. Do you have any thoughts on what could be going on here? Please see the image attached.
>
> I don't think I'm familiar enough with the theory/reasoning of this method to offer anything meaningful. Perhaps others on this forum who are more familiar with the GGUM can offer some interpretation of this phenomenon?
>
> Phil
>
